explanations.simpleExplanation: HDL (high-density lipoprotein) is often called "good cholesterol". It carries cholesterol away from arteries back to the liver. Higher HDL levels are generally associated with lower cardiovascular risk.

explanations.simpleExplanation: Triglycerides are a type of fat in your blood, stored after eating excess calories. High triglycerides can contribute to hardening of arteries and are often associated with other metabolic risk factors.

explanations.simpleExplanation: Haemoglobin is the protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from your lungs to every part of your body. Low haemoglobin (anaemia) can cause tiredness, breathlessness, and pale skin.

explanations.simpleExplanation: White blood cells (WBC) are the cells of your immune system that fight infection and foreign substances. Different types (neutrophils, lymphocytes, etc.) each have specific roles.

explanations.simpleExplanation: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) is often called "bad cholesterol". High LDL levels are associated with fatty plaque buildup in arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attack and stroke.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Diet, physical activity, weight, genetics, and medications such as statins all affect LDL. If calculated using the Friedewald formula, very high triglycerides make the result unreliable.
clinicianQuestions: Is my LDL calculated or measured directly?

explanations.simpleExplanation: HDL (high-density lipoprotein) is often called "good cholesterol". It carries cholesterol away from arteries back to the liver. Higher HDL levels are generally associated with lower cardiovascular risk.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Regular aerobic exercise, moderate alcohol consumption, smoking cessation, and certain medications can raise HDL. Obesity, physical inactivity, and high triglycerides tend to lower it.
clinicianQuestions: What lifestyle changes could help improve my HDL level if it is low?

explanations.simpleExplanation: Triglycerides are a type of fat in your blood, stored after eating excess calories. High triglycerides can contribute to hardening of arteries and are often associated with other metabolic risk factors.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Eating shortly before the test, alcohol consumption, uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid conditions, kidney disease, and certain medications can all raise triglycerides significantly.
clinicianQuestions: Was this test done fasting? If not, should I repeat it fasting?

explanations.simpleExplanation: Fasting blood glucose is the amount of sugar (glucose) in your blood after not eating for at least 8 hours. Glucose is the main fuel your body uses for energy. The pancreas produces insulin to help cells absorb glucose.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Stress, illness, very recent exercise, certain medications (steroids, some blood-pressure drugs), and the timing of the last meal can all affect fasting glucose. A single measurement can vary day-to-day.
clinicianQuestions: Is my fasting glucose result from a capillary (finger-prick) or venous (arm draw) sample?
Should I repeat this test on another day to confirm the result?
Are any of my current medications known to affect blood sugar?

explanations.simpleExplanation: HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) reflects your average blood glucose level over the past 2-3 months. Glucose attaches to haemoglobin (a protein in red blood cells), and this percentage reflects how much attachment has occurred.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Anaemia, blood transfusions, certain haemoglobin variants, kidney disease, and some supplements can make HbA1c less reliable. It is an average and does not show daily fluctuations.
clinicianQuestions: Does my haemoglobin level or any variant affect how accurate this HbA1c reading is?
How often should I monitor HbA1c given my current result?

explanations.simpleExplanation: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation or infection. Elevated CRP indicates inflammation somewhere in the body but does not pinpoint the cause.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Any infection, injury, chronic inflammation, or autoimmune condition can raise CRP. High-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) is used specifically for cardiovascular risk assessment.
clinicianQuestions: Is this a standard CRP or a high-sensitivity (hs-CRP) result?
What is the likely source of inflammation given my symptoms?

clinicianQuestions: Does my post-meal glucose rise indicate impaired glucose tolerance?
Should I monitor my blood sugar before and after specific meals?

explanations.simpleExplanation: Fasting Insulin measures resting insulin secretion from the pancreas. Elevated fasting insulin indicates underlying metabolic insulin resistance even if blood glucose remains in normal range.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Acute dietary intake, physical inactivity, sleep deprivation, and body composition alter fasting insulin.
clinicianQuestions: Does my fasting insulin indicate insulin resistance, and would dietary modifications help?

explanations.simpleExplanation: HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance) mathematically relates fasting glucose and fasting insulin. A score above 2.0 indicates reduced insulin sensitivity.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Strict 8-12 hour fasting is required for mathematically valid HOMA-IR calculation.
clinicianQuestions: What lifestyle interventions or medical therapies are recommended for my HOMA-IR score?

explanations.simpleExplanation: C-Peptide is created when insulin is produced by the pancreas. Measuring C-peptide shows how much endogenous insulin your body is making on its own.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Fasting status, kidney clearance, and pancreatic beta-cell function influence circulating C-peptide concentrations.
clinicianQuestions: What does my C-peptide level reveal about my pancreas beta-cell reserve?

explanations.simpleExplanation: Fructosamine reflects average blood glucose control over the past 2 to 3 weeks by measuring glycated serum proteins (mainly albumin).
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Useful when HbA1c is unreliable due to hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, or recent blood loss/transfusions.
clinicianQuestions: Why was fructosamine measured instead of or in addition to HbA1c?

explanations.simpleExplanation: HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) reflects your average blood glucose level over the past 2-3 months. Glucose attaches to haemoglobin (a protein in red blood cells), and this percentage reflects how much attachment has occurred.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Anaemia, blood transfusions, certain haemoglobin variants, kidney disease, and some supplements can make HbA1c less reliable. It is an average and does not show daily fluctuations.
clinicianQuestions: Does my haemoglobin level or any variant affect how accurate this HbA1c reading is?
How often should I monitor HbA1c given my current result?

explanations.simpleExplanation: Estimated Average Glucose (eAG) translates your HbA1c percentage into the familiar daily mg/dL units used on fingerstick glucose meters over the preceding 2 to 3 months.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Derived directly from HbA1c using the ADAG formula: eAG (mg/dL) = 28.7 × HbA1c - 46.7.
clinicianQuestions: How closely does this eAG match my daily home blood glucose meter readings?

explanations.simpleExplanation: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) is produced by the pituitary gland to control thyroid activity. A high TSH often suggests the thyroid is underactive; a low TSH may suggest it is overactive. TSH is typically the first thyroid test ordered.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Time of day (TSH peaks at night), recent illness, medications (including steroids, amiodarone, lithium, and biotin), pregnancy, and pituitary conditions can all affect TSH levels. Reference ranges vary between laboratories.
clinicianQuestions: Should Free T4 and/or Free T3 be checked alongside this TSH result?
Are any of my medications known to affect thyroid hormone levels?
Has this TSH been measured on a specific time of day or after any change in medication?

explanations.simpleExplanation: Free T4 (thyroxine) is the main thyroid hormone in circulation that is not bound to proteins. Together with TSH, it gives a fuller picture of thyroid function.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Severe illness, protein abnormalities, and certain medications can affect Free T4 levels. Reference ranges differ between different laboratory assays and pregnancy.
clinicianQuestions: How does my Free T4 level relate to my TSH result?
Does my laboratory use the same reference range for pregnancy?

explanations.simpleExplanation: Free T3 (triiodothyronine) is the active form of thyroid hormone. It is usually checked when TSH and Free T4 are abnormal to gain additional information about thyroid status.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: T3 can be low in severe non-thyroid illness even without true thyroid disease. It fluctuates more during the day than T4.
clinicianQuestions: Is my Free T3 result consistent with my other thyroid values?

explanations.simpleExplanation: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) is often called "bad cholesterol". High LDL levels are associated with fatty plaque buildup in arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attack and stroke.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Diet, physical activity, weight, genetics, and medications such as statins all affect LDL. If calculated using the Friedewald formula, very high triglycerides make the result unreliable.
clinicianQuestions: Is my LDL calculated or measured directly?

explanations.simpleExplanation: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation or infection. Elevated CRP indicates inflammation somewhere in the body but does not pinpoint the cause.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Any infection, injury, chronic inflammation, or autoimmune condition can raise CRP. High-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) is used specifically for cardiovascular risk assessment.
clinicianQuestions: Is this a standard CRP or a high-sensitivity (hs-CRP) result?
What is the likely source of inflammation given my symptoms?

explanations.simpleExplanation: Fasting blood glucose is the amount of sugar (glucose) in your blood after not eating for at least 8 hours. Glucose is the main fuel your body uses for energy. The pancreas produces insulin to help cells absorb glucose.
explanations.limitationsAndFactors: Stress, illness, very recent exercise, certain medications (steroids, some blood-pressure drugs), and the timing of the last meal can all affect fasting glucose. A single measurement can vary day-to-day.
clinicianQuestions: Is my fasting glucose result from a capillary (finger-prick) or venous (arm draw) sample?
